descriptionChirho: To turn oneself around bodily, to wheel about or face a different direction. This is the most frequent NT use of strepho, appearing predominantly in the passive/middle aorist participle strapheis ('having turned') as a narrative marker of physical reorientation before speaking. Jesus turns to address Peter (Matt 16:23), turns to look at the woman who touched him (Matt 9:22), turns to address crowds and disciples (Luke 7:9, 7:44, 9:55, 10:23, 14:25, 22:61, 23:28), turns in John's Gospel (John 1:38, 20:14, 20:16), and the Israelites turned back to Egypt (Acts 7:39). The Hebrew equivalent is consistently panah (to turn, face). This sense covers concrete bodily rotation or change of facing direction.

To turn or direct something, to cause a change or transformation in an object or substance, used transitively with an external object rather than reflexively. In Matthew 5:39, Jesus commands turning the other cheek, directing one's body part toward the striker. In Revelation 11:6, the two witnesses have power to turn waters into blood. The Hebrew equivalents hapneh (direct/turn) and lahafokh (to overturn/transform) capture this causative, transitive sense. Unlike the intransitive physical turning sense, here the subject causes something else to be turned or changed, emphasizing agency over an external object or material.

To bring back or return something to its original place or owner. In Matthew 27:3, Judas returned (estrep sen) the thirty pieces of silver to the chief priests and elders after regretting his betrayal of Jesus. The Hebrew equivalent heshiv (to return, restore) and the multilingual glosses (Arabic arja'a, Spanish devolvio, Hindi lautaya) all confirm a sense of restitution or giving back rather than mere physical rotation. This specialized use of strepho for returning an object distinguishes it from both the physical turning and the metaphorical/spiritual conversion senses.

To turn back in a spiritual or moral sense, to undergo conversion or repentance, turning from one spiritual orientation to another. In Matthew 18:3, Jesus says 'unless you turn and become like children,' using strepho for spiritual transformation. In John 12:40, the people's hearts are hardened so that they may not turn (and be healed), referring to spiritual repentance. In Acts 13:46, Paul and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles, redirecting their missionary focus. The Hebrew equivalents tashuvu (you shall return/repent) and ponim (turning/facing) connect to the rich OT theology of teshuvah (repentance as turning). This metaphorical extension from physical turning to spiritual reorientation is a distinct lexicographic sense.
